# A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence: full text of the site

> 91 concepts of artificial intelligence, one page each, in plain language. A book written with AI, which says so, and read critically by a peer.

A book by Stéphane Vial. Available October 13, 2026. Foreword by Marcello Vitali-Rosati. ISBN 978-2-9825534-2-2 (print) and 978-2-9825534-3-9 (ePUB). ## A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/

Stéphane Vial · Available October 13, 2026 · Foreword by Marcello Vitali-Rosati

I wrote a book about AI, with AI, and I explain how. Ninety-one concepts, one page each, to understand what artificial intelligence is and how it works.

As with any scholarly publication, every page was read and critically commented on by a peer. Marcello Vitali-Rosati, Full Professor at the Université de Montréal, took on that role and wrote the foreword.

But that is not all: I also produced and published this book with the help of AI, from the cover to the marketing, by way of the legal deposit. The last four pages tell how I went about it.

S.V., Montréal, October 2026

### Three things to read on this site

- **[Eight excerpts](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/)**  
  Artificial Intelligence · Neuron · Machine Learning · Natural Language Processing · Token · Hallucination · Recommender System · Agentic AI

### The author

**Stéphane Vial**, Ph.D., is a Full Professor at the School of Design of the Université du Québec à Montréal, a regular researcher at the IUSMM Research Centre and the founder of Mentallys Inc. He holds a PhD in philosophy, a degree in clinical psychology and a habilitation to supervise research in design, and teaches, among other things, the use of artificial intelligence in research, writing and creative work.

The author of several books, including *Being and the Screen: How the Digital Changes Perception* (MIT Press), he explores how technologies transform our ways of perceiving, thinking and acting.

## 91 concepts to understand artificial intelligence

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/

Eight chapters, eight entries to read

Artificial intelligence answers our questions, completes our sentences, creates images and organizes our access to information. It is everywhere, but what do we really know about how it works? What is a model? How does a machine learn? What are a token, a vector, fine-tuning or a hallucination?

This living lexicon offers a clear, rigorous and accessible introduction, free of fantasies and easy fears. Organized in thematic chapters, it reads like a story: from the most fundamental to the most applied, from inside the models to their effects on the world.

### The eight chapters

#### 1. What Artificial Intelligence Is

**Before getting into technical detail, let’s start with the basics. What is artificial intelligence?** (15 concepts)

Imitation Game · Artificial Intelligence · Generative Artificial Intelligence · Algorithm · Model · Phases (of a Model) · Training · Inference · Fine-Tuning · Foundation Model · Agent · Alignment · Transparency · Explainability · Open Source

- Excerpt to read: [Artificial Intelligence](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/artificial-intelligence/) · page 22

#### 2. What an AI System Contains: Neurons and Parameters

**Inside every artificial intelligence lies a complex mathematical structure: neurons, weights, functions, layers, and so on.** (16 concepts)

Perceptron · Neuron · Parameter · Weight · Bias (Parameter) · Activation Function · Layer · Neural Network · Backpropagation · Attention · Transformer · Language Model · Large Language Model · Reasoning Model · Diffusion Model · Multimodal

- Excerpt to read: [Neuron](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/neuron/) · page 40

#### 3. What (and How) AI Learns: Forms of Learning

**An AI system is not programmed in the classic sense of the word: it learns. But what does learning mean for a machine?** (11 concepts)

Learning · Machine Learning · Supervised Learning · Unsupervised Learning · Reinforcement Learning · Deep Learning · Dataset · Training Data · Personal Data · Pattern · Overfitting

- Excerpt to read: [Machine Learning](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/machine-learning/) · page 58

#### 4. What AI “Understands”: Language, Images, Sound

**Artificial intelligence does more than process numbers: it handles language, analyzes images, recognizes voices.** (9 concepts)

Natural Language Processing · Chatbot · Generative Pre-trained Transformer · Machine Translation · Speech Recognition · Text-to-Speech · Computer Vision · Facial Recognition · Image Generator

- Excerpt to read: [Natural Language Processing](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/natural-language-processing/) · page 71

#### 5. The Language of Models: Tokens and Computation

**What does an AI system “see” when it reads a word, an image or a sentence? It does not understand the way a human does: it computes.** (6 concepts)

Token · Context Window · Vector · Probability · SoftMax · Temperature

- Excerpt to read: [Token](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/token/) · page 83

#### 6. What AI Produces: Answers, Errors, Hallucinations

**AI answers, predicts, generates. But it can also get things wrong, distort or invent.** (12 concepts)

Input / Output · Prompt · Chain of Thought · Retrieval-Augmented Generation · Context Drift · Hallucination · Algorithmic Bias · Over-elaboration · Sycophancy · Black Box · Prompt Injection · Deepfake

- Excerpt to read: [Hallucination](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/hallucination/) · page 96

#### 7. AI in Our Digital Lives: Filters, Engines, Interfaces

**Artificial intelligence structures our everyday digital uses: it filters, ranks, recommends, moderates.** (10 concepts)

Personalization · News Feed · Recommender System · Collaborative Filtering · Ranking · Content Moderation · Spam Detection · Filter Bubble · Latency · Vibe Coding

- Excerpt to read: [Recommender System](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/recommender-system/) · page 107

#### 8. Where Is Artificial Intelligence Going? Horizons, Risks, Questions

**Artificial intelligence is advancing quickly, and with it come decisive questions.** (12 concepts)

Computing Power · Agentic AI · Artificial General Intelligence · Consciousness (Sentience) · AI Scheming · AI Psychosis · Existential Risk · AI Ecological Impact · AI Race · Sovereign AI · AI Governance · Responsible AI

- Excerpt to read: [Agentic AI](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/agentic-ai/) · page 118

### How to cite this book

Vial, S. (2026). *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence*. Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

## The Making of This Book

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/making-of/

How this book was conceived, written, checked, produced and published, without giving up any of my intellectual standards.

The first idea for this book goes back to the moment when, like many others, I realized that artificial intelligence could do the thing I love most faster than I can: writing. I did not say better than me. I said faster. Writing is labour, intellectual and cognitive of course, but also craft and handwork: fingers on the keyboard or on paper, a little like the work of a painter, who knows their pigments and lays down the layers one by one on the canvas. I wanted to run an experiment, to see what it is to write with a new instrument said to be so powerful. Do I really need, I asked myself, to write out every determiner myself, by hand, to adjust every conjugation, to form the letters of every preposition, every relative pronoun, every coordinating conjunction?

I understood later what is happening. An author who writes with AI is like a painter who makes colour with photography: they no longer have to manufacture each pigment or lay it on the canvas by hand, but they go on thinking through and about the image they are photographing, considering the light, choosing the key colours they want to render, the framing, the sharpness, the depth of field, not to mention all the later corrections they will make with editing software. With writing it is the same. I am the one, and I will always be the one — the author — who conceives the text, works out the idea, weighs the structure and the argument, chooses the key concepts, validates the choice of every word, decides on the style, the tone, the register, and who makes the corrections in the final text. For that, I do not need to shape each letter myself or to compose the words by hand, one letter after another. My value lies elsewhere — and so does my pleasure. The instrument changes with the times; it can never be the author. The author endures through the ages; the author can only be human. Instruments have powers, but they have no identity, no intention, no signature.

Why a lexicon? Because I love dictionaries, and I have just written and edited one on design, with the help of nearly a hundred colleagues. Why artificial intelligence? Because I am the author of *Being and the Screen: How the Digital Changes Perception* (MIT Press), and because the “AI revolution” reproduces exactly the phenomenon I described for the “digital revolution”: any new technology that takes hold systemically ends up being naturalized. AI lexicons already exist, of course. I wanted to bring something different. And so came the idea that governs the whole book: a lexicon presented not in alphabetical order but in chapters, like an essay that tells a story, from the most theoretical to the most applied.

At first, I was tempted to go fast. To let AI produce, and to head straight for the result. I could not. My name on a cover has always meant the same thing, for all my books: the commitment of my intellectual and academic responsibility, the endorsement of the content word for word and, of course, my author’s signature — with the family name it carries. So it very quickly became unthinkable to let AI run without my controlling everything. I built my writing process accordingly, so as to make AI my cognitive and editorial assistant, in every one of *my* phases of work.

First, I worked out an angle, a title, and asked it to challenge me and assess me. I defined a template for the entries, and asked it, iteratively, to apply it. I had it write first drafts, which I systematically modified, sometimes a great deal, sometimes barely. I then had those drafts reread and criticized by the machine itself, which found, after the fact, problems in what it had generated. Nothing that might strike me as intelligent in its answers was intelligent in itself: when there was intelligence in them, it was because *I* was the one seeing it. I decided to ignore whole swaths of its answers; I did not even read everything it replied; I selected only what *I* found relevant, the way I read a book, taking from its contents what interests me.

And then, of course, there was the checking. I have never corrected and verified a manuscript so much. I checked every technical claim against outside sources: encyclopedias, dictionaries, scholarly articles, the websites of digital industry companies, cutting-edge posts on social media… Very often I replaced the examples it proposed with others I found more apt. I rewrote any number of turns of phrase I did not like, either because they did not sound like me, or because they smacked too much of the style of a probabilistic machine (generalizing, abstract, blandly accurate, without personality).

When I had finished the manuscript, I did what any good academic does: I asked a peer for a critical reading, and for that I chose Professor Marcello Vitali-Rosati, not because he is a friend, but because everyone knows that the way he looks at artificial intelligence is critical and uncompromising, free of any indulgence. I then had a series of corrections to make. When I again believed the final manuscript was finished, I had it analyzed by an artificial intelligence system other than the one used at the outset. I asked it to run systematic checks on every aspect of the manuscript, sometimes with several agents running in parallel: spelling and grammar, typos, accuracy (are there errors?), consistency (do I contradict myself?), terminological stability (do I use the same terms everywhere for the same things?), the makeup of the file, the page numbers, the styles, and so on. I still had to make many corrections, because inconsistencies kept appearing that I had not seen before.

Then something unexpected happened. With the manuscript finished, I discovered that I could keep going: design the cover and calculate the width of the spine; obtain the ISBNs and generate the matching barcodes; generate the index and check the ninety-one cross-references automatically; set a price grid across eight marketplaces; submit, correct the proofs, publish, promote. What a publishing house does, with its many professions and its years of know-how, I learned and carried out alone, in a few weeks. I draw no triumphant lesson from it: it was a great deal of work. Working this way demands constant vigilance.

The paradox is that producing this book took me longer than expected, but less time than a conventional publishing process would have. I had to face a few technical costs, and to develop an over-checking mindset. Choosing self-publishing also has a social cost: doing everything yourself means giving up bookstore sales representation, conventional distribution, an editorial team whose worth I know. In exchange, I gained control of the chain and total freedom, indispensable for carrying out such an experiment.

Such is the story of this book about AI, written with AI.

### Read also

[My statement on the use of artificial intelligence](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/statement/)

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). The making of this book. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (pp. 131–134). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

## Statement on the Use of Artificial Intelligence

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/statement/

“I did not write this book in spite of AI. I wrote it with AI.” The position I stand by.

This book was written with the help of artificial intelligence.

But also with the insufferable Microsoft Word and its spellchecker, the splendid Google Sheets and its way with tables, the marvellous copy-and-paste and *cut-and-paste*, search engines, Wikipedia, French-language dictionaries (CNRTL, OQLF), specialized websites such as those of IBM, Oracle or Amazon Web Services, several hundred Google searches, at least as many articles and exchanges on LinkedIn, not to mention the endless discussions with my friend Éric Kavanagh or the provocative prodding of my colleague Marcello Vitali-Rosati, who agreed to be the critical reader of this book and whose remarks brought many improvements.

In other words, this book was written the way most serious texts are written today: through an ecosystem of tools, documents, software, sources, conversations and assorted mediations.

ChatGPT and Claude were used at many stages: to explore avenues, propose terms, discuss definitions, test formulations, criticize certain passages, suggest improvements, spot ambiguities, rephrase sentences, apply systematic corrections, prepare the final manuscript, and so on. But these systems were only an aid, and never exercised an author’s judgment over the content of the book, its structure, its approach, its conceptual choices, its final wording. Those decisions belong to the author. The systems’ proposals were systematically assessed, verified, accepted, modified or rejected.

I did not write this book in spite of AI. I wrote it with AI.

And, to be honest, I have no idea whether it took me more or less time in the end than it would have without AI, so many hundreds of times did I go back and forth between my thoughts, tools, documents, sources, conversations with AI, conversations with colleagues, online exchanges, notes taken and other bursts of inspiration in the shower… No prompt could have generated this book.

Like every intellectual technology before it — from the clay tablet to the printed book, from the word processor to the search engine — AI has become one working instrument among others, at least for those who do not want to give up their capacity to think and who have understood that there is no prompt magic.

AI does not do away with the work of writing: it inserts a new layer of labour, faster and more efficient in some respects but no less intellectually demanding and laborious, whether in ideation, structuring, background research, putting into words, rephrasing, correcting or proofreading — and all of this without ever taking the place of the author, in order, finally, to stimulate us and push us towards even higher standards.

If some pages of this book strike you as illuminating, the credit goes to the quality of the intellectual work I put into them. If they strike you as questionable or inaccurate, the responsibility is likewise mine.

Artificial intelligence can assist with writing. It never exempts us from thinking.

### Read also

[The Making of This Book](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/making-of/)

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Statement on the use of artificial intelligence. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (pp. 129–130). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

## A Montréal professor publishes a book about AI, written with AI

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/press-release/

Press release

Montréal, October 2026

Stéphane Vial, Full Professor at the School of Design of the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM), publishes *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence*: ninety-one concepts, one page each, to better understand AI and how it works.

Not only was the book written with AI, it also documents the process. The last four pages tell how the author went about writing with AI without ever giving up his intellectual standards: “I did not say it could do so better than me. I said faster,” he writes.

The foreword and critical reading are by Marcello Vitali-Rosati, Full Professor at the Université de Montréal. Peer review is the foundation of scholarly publishing, and writing with AI changes strictly nothing about that.

The book is self-published, as a creative and exploratory choice. Such a writing experiment, rather ahead of its time, required complete freedom. What is more, with the help of AI, the author went further still and ran the whole chain himself, from the cover to the legal deposit, and accepted the price: no bookshops, no distribution, no editorial team.

The book is aimed in particular at teachers and students in every discipline, who now have to talk about AI before having had the time to study it. It ends with these words: “Artificial intelligence can assist with writing. It never exempts us from thinking.”

The English edition is translated from the French; the translation was revised by Alexia Moyer. The original, *Petit lexique vivant de l’intelligence artificielle*, was published on October 6, 2026.

**Stéphane Vial** is a Full Professor at the School of Design of UQAM and a regular researcher at the IUSMM Research Centre. He holds a PhD in philosophy and is the author, among other books, of *Being and the Screen: How the Digital Changes Perception* (MIT Press).

### Why only on Amazon?

This book is an experiment, and that experiment could only be carried out through self-publishing. I made the deliberate choice to write a book about artificial intelligence with artificial intelligence, because I know it can be done without giving up any intellectual rigour. I did not want to have to negotiate that choice with a publishing house that would have needed convincing, at a time when AI is shaking up the cultural industries and publishers’ caution is understandable.

I did not want to depend on anyone to carry out this experiment as an author freely, to the very end. And to the very end did not only mean writing the book with AI, as I explain in “[The Making of This Book](https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/making-of/)”, but actually producing everything else: the layout, the printing, the proofreading, the ISBN, the legal deposit, the sales settings, and so on. So I had to be the publisher as well.

This book is an experiment in authorship and in publishing at once, and it required a platform that makes it possible for a single person to distribute a book worldwide, on demand, in print and digital, with no stock and no intermediary. That was the material condition of the experiment.

## Artificial Intelligence

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/artificial-intelligence/

Chapter 1 · page 22

**Definition**  
Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to a set of computational methods and systems able to reproduce or simulate certain capacities usually associated with human intelligence. For example: understanding language, recognizing images, solving problems or learning from data. This is not conscious thought, but an ability to reproduce, through calculation, certain mechanisms of human reasoning, learning and perception.

**Example**  
When we ask a voice assistant for the weather, or when Netflix recommends a series, we are already using AI systems. These tools analyze our requests, identify patterns in our habits and draw on models trained at scale to produce a relevant answer, without our needing to know anything about programming.

**Why it matters**  
AI is transforming many fields: health, finance, education, sports, transport, artistic creation… It makes it possible to automate certain tasks and to extend human capacities, but it also creates new social, ethical and political risks. Understanding what artificial intelligence is means fantasizing less about its nature, being more realistic, and making better decisions about how we want to use it.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Artificial Intelligence. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 22). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

## Neuron

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/neuron/

Chapter 2 · page 40

**Definition**  
An artificial neuron is a computing unit whose name and general principle are borrowed, in simplified form, from biological neurons. In the human brain, a biological neuron receives signals (through its dendrites), combines them (in the cell body) and passes on, or does not pass on, a signal to other neurons. In a similar way, an artificial neuron receives one or more inputs, performs a calculation (usually a weighted sum), applies an activation function, then produces an output. The calculation it performs makes it possible to detect patterns.

**Example**  
In an image recognition model, thousands of artificial neurons are organized into layers. The neurons in the first layers detect simple shapes (lines, colours), those in the middle layers recognize patterns (eyes, wheels), and those in the final layers identify the whole object (cat, car). Each neuron “activates” or “inhibits” the passing of information (to the next neuron) according to what it has learned.

**Why it matters**  
The artificial neuron is a fundamental building block of deep learning. It is the arrangement and the adjustment of millions (even billions) of neurons, organized into networks, that give a model its capacity to analyze, to predict or to generate.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Neuron. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 40). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

---

## Machine Learning

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/machine-learning/

Chapter 3 · page 58

**Definition**  
Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence that lets a system learn from data rather than being programmed rule by rule. We give it examples, and it automatically adjusts its parameters to fit them. From them it extracts statistical patterns that it can reuse on new data. It is currently the dominant approach to designing high-performing AI systems.

**Example**  
To train a speech recognition system, we have it listen to thousands of hours of recordings along with their transcripts. The model learns to match sounds to words, and can then transcribe sentences it has never heard, because it has picked up the statistical patterns of language. This type of learning is generally supervised: each example comes with the “right answer”, which guides the model as it adjusts.

**Why it matters**  
Nearly all of today’s AI relies on machine learning: facial recognition, spam filters, recommendations, voice assistants, and so on. This is a profound shift: we no longer describe the solution explicitly, we let the model discover it from the data. These systems, however, lack human-like understanding; they produce results from calculations and probabilities. That distinction helps us to grasp both their power… and their limits.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Machine Learning. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 58). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

---

## Natural Language Processing

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/natural-language-processing/

Chapter 4 · page 71

**Definition**  
Natural language processing refers to a set of computational methods that allow a machine to process, interpret and produce human language, written or spoken. It is a field of research that has developed since the 1950s, at the crossroads of linguistics, computer science and, today, machine learning. Language is converted into usable data (words, sentences, structures), then analyzed by models in order to produce coherent results from the patterns detected.

**Example**  
When you use a search engine, the system interprets your query, identifies the important words and sometimes infers your intent in order to offer relevant results. In the same way, machine translation tools and chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude analyze sentence structure to produce a response suited to the context. These systems do not work on isolated words: they take in the whole sentence and its surroundings.

**Why it matters**  
Natural language processing has become a central interface between humans and machines. It allows for more direct interaction, without going through technical commands. But language remains ambiguous, contextual and culturally situated, which limits performance: models can produce plausible answers without really grasping meaning, which explains certain errors and misunderstandings.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Natural Language Processing. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 71). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

---

## Token

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/token/

Chapter 5 · page 83

**Definition**  
In artificial intelligence, a token is the smallest unit of text that language models handle. It can be a whole word, a fragment of a word, a punctuation mark or a space, depending on how each model does its splitting. Rather than reading continuous sentences, the model receives an ordered sequence of tokens, each converted into a numerical representation before being processed. Generative models also produce their answers token by token, in an extremely fast probabilistic chain.

**Example**  
The sentence *Hello, how are you?* could be split into six tokens: *Hello* + *,* + *how* + *are* + *you* + *?*. Some words can be divided further: *tokenization* would become *token* + *ization*. In applications such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, which run on large language models, every question sent and every answer generated is counted in tokens. That count determines the length limits of a conversation, the processing speed and often the cost of use.

**Why it matters**  
The token is the basic unit of operation for language models. The context window, too, is expressed in tokens, not in words. This logic has concrete effects: the same text does not yield the same number of tokens from one language to another. The cost of using models is in fact generally calculated based on the number of tokens processed, input as well as output. Understanding what a token is therefore helps you grasp how an AI system “reads” and generates text, but also why some requests cost more in computation and in energy.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Token. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 83). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

---

## Hallucination

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/hallucination/

Chapter 6 · page 96

**Definition**  
A hallucination is the phenomenon by which a model generates false, invented, distorted or misleading information while presenting it with apparent coherence or confidence. Language models can thus produce answers that are credible, well written and convincing… but factually wrong. This follows from the very way a probabilistic model works: it does not check whether what it asserts is true; it simply predicts the most plausible continuation of words, given its training and the context of the conversation.

**Example**  
Ask a chatbot to cite sources on a highly specialized subject and it may invent references that do not exist: “According to a study by Miller published in 2017 in the journal *Health and Cognition*…”, when neither the study nor even the journal cited exists. In the same way, an AI system can attribute a quotation to the wrong person, invent a court ruling or describe an imaginary feature of a piece of software. The more ambiguous, rare or hard to verify the request, the greater the risk of hallucination.

**Why it matters**  
Hallucinations can be harmless in a humorous context, but troublesome in sensitive fields such as health, education or law. To limit them, current systems use various approaches: better training, access to up-to-date external sources, RAG-type architectures, and so on. These techniques can improve the reliability of answers, but they do not turn a probabilistic model into a fact-checking system. A convincing answer must therefore always be assessed critically.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Hallucination. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 96). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

---

## Recommender System

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/recommender-system/

Chapter 7 · page 107

**Definition**  
A recommender system is an algorithmic system designed to automatically offer content, products or services to a user based on their preferences, their past behaviour or that of users judged to be similar. It analyzes signals such as clicks, searches, purchases, views or time spent on certain content in order to anticipate what might hold the user’s attention. These systems are everywhere: on streaming platforms, online retail, social media and music apps.

**Example**  
On a video streaming platform, the recommender system suggests films or series based on your viewing history and on the behaviour of users whose profiles are close to yours. On an e-commerce platform, it offers products related to your purchases or to those of similar customers.

**Why it matters**  
Recommender systems filter the immense quantity of information available online and influence our choices, often without our being fully aware of it. Well calibrated, they help us discover content that is relevant or suited to our tastes. But because they also seek to maximize attention and engagement, they can favour emotional, polarizing or repetitive content. At scale, they therefore play a major role in how we inform ourselves, how we consume and even how we perceive the digital world.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Recommender System. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 107). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.

---

## Agentic AI

Address: https://web.stephane-vial.net/lexique-ia/en/book/agentic-ai/

Chapter 8 · page 118

**Definition**  
Agentic AI refers to artificial intelligence systems capable of acting semi-autonomously or autonomously to reach a goal, often over several steps. Unlike a standard chatbot, which merely answers an immediate request, an agentic AI can plan actions, use tools, access external services, remember certain information and adjust its behaviour according to the results it obtains. In practice, this autonomy rests on a language model orchestrated with instructions, a memory and tools. The whole then behaves like an agent carrying out tasks with little human supervision.

**Example**  
An AI agent asked to organize a trip can search for flights, compare hotels, check the weather, book activities, fill in forms and send confirmations by email, all from an instruction such as: “Organize a weekend in Rome for two people in May.” Claude Code is an example of an advanced software agent. It can write code, modify files, run commands, call external tools and chain several actions together to reach a defined goal.

**Why it matters**  
Agentic AI no longer merely generates content or answers questions: it can chain several actions together using tools and software. This capacity opens up significant possibilities for automation in work, services and research. But that autonomy also raises critical issues of safety, control and responsibility.

### How to cite this text

Vial, S. (2026). Agentic AI. In *A Living Lexicon of Artificial Intelligence* (p. 118). Stéphane Vial, publisher, Montréal.
